articles.text: Throughout 2020 I have been amazed at how this year has invited me deeper into the stories of faith. When the pandemic arrived, forcing us to isolate, I sadly, but somewhat jokingly, told my congregation, “I bet you never thought you would give up church for Lent.” We all felt this dread that we were being thrown out of our usual orbit and might lose the gravitational pull of faith. articles.text: Total cases in Piedmont soars to 80 As the first doses of a COVID- 19 vaccine arrive in the San Francisco Bay Area, new cases of the disease are spiking in Alameda County like never before. The first doses of a COVID-19 vaccine manufactured by Pfizer will arrive in Alameda County in the next few days, health officials announced on Monday, December 14. The first people to be vaccinated will include hospital workers and 911 responders at highest risk of exposure. “While we are still in the early phases, this is a hopeful moment for Alameda County residents,” Alameda County Board of Supervisors President Richard Valle said in a statement. “A safe and effective vaccine will save lives and help residents and businesses return to some level of normalcy.” The county expects to receive 12,675 doses. More doses are anticipated to arrive in the coming weeks. “Acute care hospital health care workers and 911 first responders at highest risk for exposure to COVID-19 are our first line of defense in protecting our system of care from becoming overwhelmed and understaffed during this surge,” said Deputy Health Officer Dr. Kathleen Clanon. While it was not announced if any doses of the vaccine had been administered in Alameda County as of press time, several people were vaccinated at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital yesterday, Tuesday, December 15. The vaccine news comes as cases are surging to unprecedented levels in the region. On Friday, December 11, there were 1,063 new cases of COVID- 19 reported in Alameda County, the highest number of cases in a single day ever and the first time more than a thousand cases were recorded in one day. There have been several days in the past two weeks with far more new cases than the surge in August, when daily new cases were previously at their highest levels. Nine new cases of COVID-19 were reported amongst Piedmonters in the past week, a 23 percent increase since December 1. There have been 80 cases of COVID-19 in Piedmont since the pandemic began. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in the county is currently 7.6 percent, the Alameda County Department of Public Health reported yesterday, Tuesday, December 15. The total caseload in Alameda County is now 38,971, an increase of over 5,200 cases from one week ago. Tragically, 33 more people have died of COVID-19 in the county, bringing the total number of fatalities to 558. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, the number of cases has now reached 13,338. In Hayward, 6,010 cases have been recorded. There are an additional seven cities in the county each with a caseload over 1,000. A new stay-at-home order for the county went into effect on Monday, December 7. The goal is to limit in-person interactions between people from different households. Restaurants must reduce operations to take-out and delivery only; outdoor and indoor dining are both prohibited. Museums, movie theatres, zoos and personal care businesses, like hair salons, must close. Outdoor playgrounds are also now shuttered. Malls, shopping centers and retail stores can remain open with capacity restrictions. The county health order is connected to a supplemental state health order that went into effect this month due to coronavirus cases spiking across California. The state order is activated when a regional group of counties, such as the Bay Area, announces that ICU capacity has dropped below 15 percent. While the Bay Area has not reached that threshold, health authorities from five Bay Area counties agreed to adopt the stricter stay-at-home restrictions as a precaution. The health orders in the Bay Area are scheduled to remain in place until January 4 but could be extended. Before the current surge, the worst day for the pandemic in Alameda County was August 13, when 417 cases were recorded. The rising case rate caused the state last month to put the entire county into the Purple Tier, or Widespread Tier. The Purple Tier is the most restrictive tier of the state’s color-coded four-tiered system for reopening businesses and activities. As of this week, the county’s case rate is 19.8 cases per 100,000 people, a massive increase from one week ago. According to the state, counties are placed in the Purple Tier when the case rate is over 7 per 100,000 people. The state and county are urging the public to stay home, wear face masks and maintain social distancing protocols. The surge in Alameda County echoes an alarming flood of cases throughout the United States even as the first COVID-19 vaccines are being administered. articles.text: A program that lets California residents know if they have been exposed to COVID-19 was rolled out statewide last Thursday, December 10. The smartphone application, CA Notify, is available on all iPhones and Android devices. G ov. G av i n Ne w s o m announced the launch of CA Notify during a press conference last week when the application officially went live across the state. “Throughout this pandemic we have tapped California’s talent pool to fight this virus, and that includes working with tech innovators like Apple and Google,” said Gov. Newsom. “CA Notify will help slow the spread by alerting those who opt in to receive an alert if they’ve come into contact with someone who has tested positive. The process is private, anonymous and secure, and is one of the many tools in the state’s data-driven approach to help reduce the spread.” The program is voluntary and is not defined as contact tracing. It notifies users who have been in close contact with another user who has opted into the system and tested positive for the virus. When individuals voluntarily activate CA Notify, the tool uses Bluetooth technology to exchange random codes between phones without revealing the user’s identity or location. If a CA Notify user tests positive for COVID-19, they will receive a verification code to plug into the app, if they choose. Any other CA Notify users who have been within six feet for 15 minutes or more of the COVID-19 positive individual will get an anonymous notification of possible exposure. Users who have tested positive will get a text from the California Department of Public Health with a code, which they can enter into the CA Notify application, triggering an alert to phones of people who may have been exposed in the previous 14 days. Android users can download CA Notify through the application store. Apple iPhone users simply need to activate the built-in feature. Vaccine arrives in Bay Area as COVID-19 cases surge at unprecedented rates Total cases in Piedmont soars to 80 By Barry Eitel As the first doses of a COVID- 19 vaccine arrive in the San Francisco Bay Area, new cases of the disease are spiking in Alameda County like never before. The first doses of a COVID-19 vaccine manufactured by Pfizer will arrive in Alameda County in the next few days, health officials announced on Monday, December 14. The first people to be vaccinated will include hospital workers and 911 responders at highest risk of exposure. “While we are still in the early phases, this is a hopeful moment for Alameda County residents,” Alameda County Board of Supervisors President Richard Valle said in a statement. “A safe and effective vaccine will save lives and help residents and businesses return to some level of normalcy.” The county expects to receive 12,675 doses. More doses are anticipated to arrive in the coming weeks. “Acute care hospital health care workers and 911 first responders at highest risk for exposure to COVID-19 are our first line of defense in protecting our system of care from becoming overwhelmed and understaffed during this surge,” said Deputy Health Officer Dr. Kathleen Clanon. While it was not announced if any doses of the vaccine had been administered in Alameda County as of press time, several people were vaccinated at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital yesterday, Tuesday, December 15. The vaccine news comes as cases are surging to unprecedented levels in the region. On Friday, December 11, there were 1,063 new cases of COVID- 19 reported in Alameda County, the highest number of cases in a single day ever and the first time more than a thousand cases were recorded in one day. There have been several days in the past two weeks with far more new cases than the surge in August, when daily new cases were previously at their highest levels. Nine new cases of COVID-19 were reported amongst Piedmonters in the past week, a 23 percent increase since December 1. There have been 80 cases of COVID-19 in Piedmont since the pandemic began. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in the county is currently 7.6 percent, the Alameda County Department of Public Health reported yesterday, Tuesday, December 15. The total caseload in Alameda County is now 38,971, an increase of over 5,200 cases from one week ago. Tragically, 33 more people have died of COVID-19 in the county, bringing the total number of fatalities to 558. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, the number of cases has now reached 13,338. In Hayward, 6,010 cases have been recorded. There are an additional seven cities in the county each with a caseload over 1,000. A new stay-at-home order for the county went into effect on Monday, December 7. The goal is to limit in-person interactions between people from different households. Restaurants must reduce operations to take-out and delivery only; outdoor and indoor dining are both prohibited. Museums, movie theatres, zoos and personal care businesses, like hair salons, must close. Outdoor playgrounds are also now shuttered. Malls, shopping centers and retail stores can remain open with capacity restrictions. The county health order is connected to a supplemental state health order that went into effect this month due to coronavirus cases spiking across California. The state order is activated when a regional group of counties, such as the Bay Area, announces that ICU capacity has dropped below 15 percent. While the Bay Area has not reached that threshold, health authorities from five Bay Area counties agreed to adopt the stricter stay-at-home restrictions as a precaution. The health orders in the Bay Area are scheduled to remain in place until January 4 but could be extended. Before the current surge, the worst day for the pandemic in Alameda County was August 13, when 417 cases were recorded. The rising case rate caused the state last month to put the entire county into the Purple Tier, or Widespread Tier. The Purple Tier is the most restrictive tier of the state’s color-coded four-tiered system for reopening businesses and activities. As of this week, the county’s case rate is 19.8 cases per 100,000 people, a massive increase from one week ago. According to the state, counties are placed in the Purple Tier when the case rate is over 7 per 100,000 people. The state and county are urging the public to stay home, wear face masks and maintain social distancing protocols. The surge in Alameda County echoes an alarming flood of cases throughout the United States even as the first COVID-19 vaccines are being administered. articles.text: Last week, a Red Flag Warning was issued for the East Bay Hills by the National Weather Service – a rare event for December. NWS issued the Red Flag Warning, meaning critical fire weather conditions are present, from Sunday, December 6 at 11 p.m. to 5 a.m. on Monday, December 7. The impacted area encompassed the East Bay Hills, including the Oakland Hills and Berkeley Hills, as well as all of the North Bay and the interior valleys. The warning also covered the Santa Cruz Mountains and the Pacific coastline along the San Francisco Peninsula. High, gusty winds moving from the Pacific Ocean over Sunday night paired with a warm, low-humidity Monday afternoon caused the NWS to order the Red Flag Warning. There have been only two other December Red Flag Warnings in Bay Area history, both within the past decade – 2013 and 2017. At the height of the drought in California in the 2010s, Red Flag Warnings were occasionally ordered in January. Meteorologists believe it is possible the region could see some Red Flag Warnings issued next month. Rain fell in the Bay Area on Sunday, December 13, but Cal Fire has not declared the 2020 wildfire season over just yet. While wildfire season traditionally ends around November 30, risks are continuing into winter. As of this week, Cal Fire has not ordered any of its 21 units throughout California to activate winter preparations, traditionally a signal that the wildfire season for the year is done. The 2020 wildfire season will be remembered as one of the most devastating in history across California and the entire western United States. Five of the top 20 largest wildfires in state history occurred this year. The August Complex Fire, which burned in and around Mendocino National Forest, was the largest wildfire in California history and the state’s first “gigafire,” meaning a fire that burns over 1 million acres. Experts worry that global climate change is expanding California’s fire season into a year-round situation. Even when the 2020 wildfire season is declared over, the Piedmont Fire Department encourages all residents to stay vigilant and prepare for fire emergencies. articles.text: Anyone else ready to move on to a new year? As we finish another lap around the Sun, we’re closing out 2020 with a Virtual Balloon Drop New Year Celebration. You’re invited to join us virtually on Thursday, December 31 at 11 a.m. as we count down to the stroke of noon. Now more than ever, we can all come together for science… and a lot of fun! Balloon Drop has been a Chabot Space & Science Center tradition since 2000, creating a fun, day-time opportunity for families to celebrate the new year without staying up past their bedtime. This year, the party continues with STEM activities, a dance party, a family-friendly toast and the colorful live balloon drop spectacle. To keep the party fun and safe for learners of all ages, the Balloon Drop New Year’s Celebration will be hosted virtually this year. With so many celebrations put on hold during the COVID crisis, Chabot’s team was determined to create a magical moment for families at home this year. How do we know that Balloon Drop can still be fun at home? Well, we’ve already seen it. Back in 2018, a Chabot member was able to pull off an at-home Balloon Drop for her son. After her child came down with a stomach bug the day of the event, Chabot member Genie was able to create her own at-home party, pulling together a large bag of Happy Birthday balloons Kids celebrate the Chabot Space and Science Center annual New Year’s Eve Balloon Drop. and set herself up at the top of the stairs with the kids down below. Their family counted down and at the stroke of noon… they celebrated by releasing bouncing balloons down the staircase! And her son loved it, counting along and cheering with excitement! Right now, we’re finding more innovative ways than ever to come together. This year, our entire community has gotten creative as we celebrate milestones, holidays and more in new ways. We’ve seen drive-thru parades, live-streamed weddings and so many more new avenues of connection. While we’ll dearly miss the hundreds of smiling faces waiting eagerly for balloons to drop from our ceiling this year, our party will continue. Our community will still share a toast, a dance party, a countdown and, of course…a Balloon Drop! Together, we look forward to welcoming 2021 with excitement and optimism. During such a challenging year, we hope you’ll join us for a moment of joy and learning. Let’s say hello to a new year with one last party and a big ‘thank you’ to science! From all of us at Chabot Space & Science Center – Happy New Year! Be sure to join the Virtual Balloon Drop New Year Celebration by visiting: https://chabotspace.org/events/ events-listing/ Mary Catherine Frantz is Marketing & Communication Manager at Chabot Space and Science Center located at 10000 Skyline Blvd., in Oakland. Following the guidance from the CDC and local medical officials all in-person public programs and gatherings at the Center have been postponed or cancelled until further notice.

articles.text: Four proposals for new courses to be offered at Piedmont High School were reviewed by the school board at a first reading on December 15. Courses include Financial Literacy, Physical Computing and Robotics, Field Science Electives, and Guitar Engineering. The proposals were submitted last year by PHS teachers. Social Studies teacher Gabby Kashani proposed a new semester-long course, Financial Literacy and Personal Finance, for grades 10-12 to start next Fall. The course would cover: Behavioral Finance, Checking, Saving, Budgeting, Paying for College, Types of Credit, Investing, Insurance, and even Taxes. Many high schools offer similar courses to help prepare students for real life. Computer Science teacher Irfan Ortak proposed a yearlong course, Physical Computing and Robotics, for grades 9 and 10. Computer Science courses concerned with software have become increasingly in demand at Piedmont but Ortak has noted, “We do not currently have any course that focuses on hardware and the physical part of computing.” The course is proposed to start next fall. Science teacher Andrew Willats proposed a series of four semester-long electives focusing on Field Science for grades 9-12. “Each one would emphasize data-driven research that will allow students to assess the changes occurring in our modern world, as well as field work in and around Piedmont,” Willats wrote. The courses include: Ornithology (focusing on bird identification), Entomology (insect study), Geology, and Marine Science. These courses would start in Fall 2021 and would present low-stress upper-division course alternatives. Science teacher Marna Chamberlain has proposed a Guitar Engineering course for students in 11th and 12th grades, to begin August 2021. “This course looks at the design elements, manufacturing and assembly of solid-body electric guitars. Students will construct their own electric guitar,” she said. Students will gain building skills and life skills in the shop while practicing soldering, making circuits and using a laser cutter. articles.text: Children’s Fairyland’s famed puppeteer, Randal Metz, brought his Nutcracker puppet show to all the kids at Highlands’ Preschool in Piedmont last Friday, December 11. The school created an outdoor space for the puppet show, perhaps with fewer kids but the same love and magic that has distinguished it for decades. “[Randal] has come every year for over 20 years, and we were so sad at the thought of not being able to do it because of COVID. But he did it; he made it work. He set it up in our play yard and it was fantastic, just like always. We were so happy,” said Highlands Director Deanna Johnson. Beyond his work at Children’s Fairyland, Metz’s company, The Puppet Company, normally has 40 showings of the Nutcracker each year. But with Fairyland currently closed due to COVID, the Nutcracker puppet show was shown only once in person – at Highlands Preschool. “We were only able to do this by social distancing, with the kids on one end and me on the other, so everyone was safe about the whole thing, and I think it went really well,” Metz said. “The kids love it, just love it. Many of them have seen it year after year,” Metz added. The Nutcracker show battled through more than just a pandemic this year, as an unexpected rain threatened some the exquisitely crafted puppets. But just like real show business, the show went on with only a minor variance. “Our Chinese dragon did not breath fire like it was supposed to, it usually gives off a big smoke ring. Because it was partially raining that day, the rain foiled that. The kids asked me ‘how come the dragon did not do fire this year?’” Metz said. With or without fire the dragon impresses everyone as do so many of the characters in the performance. “There is a snow fairy that comes out in the beginning and she sprinkles iridescent snow all over where the kids are, like she is spreading it across the land. Then the little elephant comes out in The Lands of Sweets and shoots water out from his trunk. That’s definitely a fan favorite. The kids love that, it is so much fun,” Johnson recalled with a smile. Metz has been working with puppets at Children’s Fairyland in Oakland for 50 years. At the age of 10 Metz auditioned at Fairyland to be a child actor and earned the role of the Mad Hatter of Alice in Wonderland; he began apprenticing as a puppeteer with Lewis Mahlmann, who created puppet shows at Fairyland for decades. “It is all about creating good memories for them. It was really nice to visit our friends. When the kids visit Fairyland they don’t hesitate to come up to me and say, ‘You came to our school!’” Metz said. Highlands Preschool hopes to have Metz back to perform Mei Lin and the Magic Brush for Chinese New Year in February. Fairyland had to close this month due to the pandemic, but aspires to reopen its puppet theater in January. “We are anxious to get the theater up and running. The Bay Area children would love to come back and see their puppet friends again,” Metz said. Randal Metz runs the longest ongoing professional puppet theater in the United States at Children’s Fairyland In November, Metz and The Puppet Company live-streamed the Nutcracker puppet performance with the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra playing highlights from Tchaikovsky’s The Nutcracker. You can view it at: www.thesfco.org/events/ nutcracker-sweet

articles.text: A Great Conjunction of 2020 in the heavens above Clearly we have been focused on this exigent and extraordinary year. It seems counterintuitive to look up to the night sky and try and put into perspective our place and purpose in the universe. But for a singular moment we are given a unique opportunity to look toward the heavens and witness an event the likes of which has not occurred since 1226, a time when Genghis Khan rode across Asia and the renaissance was still generations away. Next week, on December 21, at 6:40 P.M. PST, Jupiter and Saturn, the two largest planets in our solar system, now remarkably close together, will appear in the southwestern night sky, just after sunset. They will seem to brightly merge in the darkened sky, absent the sun’s nimbus of light. Astronomers are calling the event the Great Conjunction. Actually this orbital alignment of these two planets began at the beginning of this year. Keep in mind that Jupiter is half a billion miles from earth and the brighter of the two; Saturn is double that distance, hence, by degrees, will appear dimmer. You will not need a telescope or binoculars to witness the Great Conjunction. The naked eye will serve budding astronomers just fine. It has been referred to it as the Christmas star, though astronomers counsel that this event, coming at the end of a long arduous year has no other astrological meaning than its rare occurrence. If you have school age children looking for a project with extrapolation potential, check out the possibilities. It’s worth a Google search for some background information.

articles.text: The song “The 12 days of Christmas” has its origins as a teaching tool to instruct young people in the meaning and content of the Christian faith. From 1558 to 1829 Roman Catholics in England were not able to practice their faith openly, so they had to find other ways to pass on their beliefs. The song is an allegory. Each of the items in the song represents something of religious significance. The hidden meaning of each gift was designed to help young Christians learn their faith. ✝ In the song “On the first day of Christmas my true love gave to me” true love represents God, and “me” is the Christian. ✝ The “partridge in a pear tree” represents Jesus Christ who died on a tree. ✝ Two turtle doves represent the Old and New Testaments. ✝ Three French hens are faith, hope and love – the three gifts of the Spirit. ✝ Four calling birds are the four Gospels. ✝ Five golden rings are the first five books of the Bible, also known as the Books of Moses. ✝ Six geese a-laying are the six days of creation. ✝ Seven swans a-swimming are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Eight maids a milking are the eight beatitudes. ✝ Nine ladies dancing are the nine fruits of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Ten lords a-leaping are the Ten Commandments. ✝ Eleven pipers piping are the eleven faithful disciples. ✝ Twelve drummers drumming are the twelve points of the Apostles’ Creed. articles.text: ’Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house Not a creature was stirring, not even a mouse. The stockings were hung by the chimney with care, In hopes that Saint Nicholas soon would be there. The children were nestled all snug in their beds, While visions of sugar plums danced in their heads; And mama in her kerchief, and I in my cap Had just settled our brains for a long winter’s nap. When out on the lawn there arose such a clatter I sprang from my bed to see what was the matter. Away to the window I flew like a flash, Tore open the shutter and threw open the sash. The moon on the breast of the new-fallen snow Gave a luster of midday to objects below; When to my wondering eyes should appear But a miniature sleigh and eight tiny reindeer. With a little old driver, so lively and quick, I knew in a moment it must be Saint Nick! More rapid than eagles his coursers they came, And he whistled and shouted and called them by name: “Now, Dasher! Now, Dancer! Now, Prancer! Now, Vixen! On, Comet! On, Cupid! On Donder and Blitzen! To the top of the porch, to the top of the wall, Now dash away, dash away, dash away all.” As dry leaves that before the wild hurricane fly, When they meet with an obstacle mount to the sky. So up to the housetop the coursers they flew, With a sleigh full of toys – and Saint Nicholas, too. And then in a twinkling, I heard on the roof The prancing and pawing of each little hoof. As I drew in my head and was turning around, Down the chimney Saint Nicholas came with a bound. He was dressed all in fur from his head to his foot, And his clothes were all tarnished with ashes and soot. A bundle of toys he had flung on his back, And he looked like a peddler just opening his pack. His eyes, how they twinkled! His dimples, how merry! His cheeks were like roses, his nose like a cherry! His droll little mouth was drawn up in a bow, And the beard on his chin was as white as the snow. The stump of a pipe he held tight in his teeth, And the smoke, it encircled his head like a wreath. He had a broad face and a little round belly That shook when he laughed like a bowl fully of jelly. He was chubby and plump, a right jolly old elf, And I laughed when I saw him in spite of myself. A wink of his eye and a twist of his head Soon gave me to know I had nothing to dread. He spoke not a word, but went straight to his work, And filled all the stockings; then turned with a jerk, And laying a finger aside of his nose, And giving a nod, up the chimney he rose. He sprang to his sleigh, to his team gave a whistle, And away they all flew like the down of a thistle. But I heard him exclaim, ’ere they drove out of sight, “Happy Christmas to all, and to all a good night!”

With the California Department of Public Health declaring that tennis can be played in Purple Tier counties, it certainly looks like girls’ tennis team could start earlier than originally planned by the CIF. “The schedule may change. The girls could start in February and the boys after that in lateApril or May. They were initially planned to start simultaneously on March 8,” said Landes. The varsity tennis team may begin workouts on Monday, January 18, but the plan for Junior Varsity tennis is still unclear. “We can’t start JV tryouts until March 8, which is quite a ways away. I know most of the players, because they are in my clinics.; he added. The future is not so rosy for boys and girls water polo, teams still in search of a pool for practices and competition. Coach John Savage confirmed that there is still considerable uncertainty with public pools still closed. “Unfortunately, I cannot provide a positive update in relation to the pools. If we were in Contra Costa County we could have in-pool workouts, but Alameda County has stricter guidelines. Laney College is likely our best bet, but they won’t let groups use their pool until students are allowed back onto campus,” he said. The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) ruled Outdoor Water Polo as a high contact sport and would require Alameda County to enter the Orange Tier in order to play. As for the possibility of playing in Contra Costa County, Savage confirmed that he has reached out to pools outside Alameda County. “At the moment, we’ve [contacted] some facilities and they are impacted as well. Everybody is looking for pool space for high school teams and club teams. Two facilities in Walnut Creek said we can have two hours on Sunday afternoons, and that was a month or two ago,” said Savage. Although the water polo teams are still searching for a pool, Savage said he is grateful the team has an opportunity to get together. “We have to wait for pools to open up. It doesn’t matter how many phone calls we put out if their response is the same. We’re grateful to be allowed to have workouts, I know some districts aren’t even allowing that. Our new A,D., Bradley Smet, has been very helpful. We’re workStaff Photos Audrey Edel is a senior on PHS girls’ tennis team. ing within the confines of a pandemic,” he added. On the track at Witter Field track, you can spot the water polo player working out to stay in shape for the time when they can finally get back int a pool – wherever it might be. “We’re currently working out at the field. We have anywhere between 15 and 20 kids showing up and our seniors are showing up as leaders. We’ve been doing a lot of individual challenges to set benchmarks, and we’re giving out awards to the highest number, fastest time, and most improved,” he said.

articles.text: The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) issued guidelines for youth and recreational adult sports on Monday, December 14, creating more disappointment for teams, athletes and coaches for a resumption of regular activity. Sports will be put into groups based on physical contact levels and the COVID risk tier in their counties. Additionally, no competition between schools will be allowed before January 25, and that date will be “reassessed” on Jan. 4. The CDPH classifies sports from “outdoor low-contact” to “indoor high-contact,” assessing that outdoor low-contact competition can be permitted on January 25, for the time being. “Inter-team competitions (i.e., between two teams) will not be allowed in California until January 25, 2021 at the earliest, based on the guidelines outlined in this document. The return-to-competition date will be reassessed by January 4, 2021 based on California disease transmission trends and is subject to change at any time given the level of COVID-19 transmission in California,” wrote the State. Piedmont High sports given the OK to compete on January 25 includes outdoor badminton, cross country, golf, swimming, tennis, and track and field. Of those sports, only cross country was scheduled to start on January 27 in the California Interscholastic Federation’s initial Season 1. Track and field, meanwhile, was set for April 25, but Piedmont High cross-country and track coach Jeanine Holmlund recently said that both sports season might be congruent.. “Just about everything is out there and what we could possibly do,” sadi Holmlund. Badminton, tennis, golf, and swimming were set to start in April according to the CIF schedule. Piedmont High tennis coach Jim Landes mentioned that the boys’ and girls’ tennis teams could return with separate schedules as in past years when the girls team played in the fall and boys’ team competed in the spring. “I was told that the schedule may change and the girls may start in February, and the boys would be after that in late April,” said Landes. The CIF Season 1 also includes football, water polo, and volleyball, all of which are likely to be changed or curtailed by the State Department of Public Health. Each sport was classified as “Outdoor High-Contact Sports,” and must enter the OOVID Orange (Moderate) Tier before returning to play. Each sport was set to start competition in January. Also in the Orange Tier designation is soccer, boys’ lacrosse, and indoor badminton for PHS teams. Taking the largest hit is boys’ and girls’ basketball, classified as a “High Contact Sport” designation; requiring Alameda County to enter the most minimal Yellow Tier—which will require a positivity rate of under two percent. Basketball, which was slated for an April 21 start, still has some time. Water polo, however, may be forced to alter its season. In Piedmont’s case, the high school will stil need to confirm that it will have aa [ppl available for practices and games. The CDPH announced that indoor water polo would also require a Yellow Tier designation, while outdoor would need Orange. For PHS, which is without a pool for its upcoming season, that means fewer options. “It does narrow things down. Other schools are also reaching around for pool space. It puts a school like Berkeley High in a tough position given they use an indoor pool,” said coach John Savage. In the Red Tier (Substantial risk), outdoor sports with moderate contact would be allowed. For Piedmont, this includes baseball, girls’ lacrosse, and softball. Each, currently, are planned to start in April as well. The State also stated that face coverings must be worn by athletes when participating in an activity. “Participants in youth and adults sports should wear face coverings when participating in the activity, even with heavy exertion as tolerated, both indoors and outdoors,” wrote the State. Another topic brought up, observers. The State plans to allow “immediate household members” to observe practices and games, but ensure that physical distance can be maintained—meaning attendance to games will be limited.

articles.text: Stanford at 3-2 opts out of bowl game, Cal season officially over A strange football season is almost over for the Pac-12 Conference. The Stanford Cardinal heads into its final game with a 3-2 record after defeating Oregon State 27-24. It is scheduled to visit UCLA on Saturday. The Cardinal at 3-2 would qualify for a post-season bowl berth, even if they were to lose to the Bruins. But the school announced that Stanford has opted out of a bowl game because the team has been off campus since December 1 as a result of Stay at Home orders prohibiting sports in Santa Clara County. “After being on the road since December 1, the Cardinal will decline postseason opportunities, the Stanford statement read. “On Monday, the program will relocate to Santa Barbara to prepare for Saturday’s game at UCLA. Stanford departed for the Seattle area on Tuesday, Dec. 1 to prepare for its road game at Washington on Dec. 5. Following that game, the program relocated on Sunday, Dec. 6 and spent the week in Corvallis, Ore. preparing for its game at Oregon State, a contest that was originally scheduled for Stanford Stadium,” wrote the school in a press release. Stanford is the first Pac-12 school to decline an invitation to the postseason. Earlier in the week, Boston College also announced it would not participate in any bowl games, as did Pittsburgh and Virginia. The Cardinal looks ahead to UCLA, which is coming off a dramatic 43-38 loss to No. 13 USC and look at Stanford as an opportunity to finish above .500, currently at 3-3. The A Stanford win will require more heroics from quarterback Davis Mills and running back Austin Jones. USC dialed up 47 pass attempts against UCLA, so you can bank on Mills getting a heavy workout. The California Golden Bears, however, had their final two games canceled after a player tested positive for COVID-19 and contact tracing protocols denied them of enough players for Washington State game last Saturday, December 12. Their game this Saturday, December 19, was officially canceled on Sunday because both Cal and the Arizona Wildcats are dealing with virus concerns. So, Cal’s tumultuous season mercifully comes to a conclusion. Its season-opener was canceled against Washington, and it got smashed 34-10 unexpectedly by UCLA. Then it relinquished the Stanford Axe back to Stanford on to a blocked PAT kick at the end of the game/ And now its final two games have been shut down. In spite of their 21-17 upset victory over Oregon on December 5, it was a season to forget. It may be worth mentioning that Cal passed up on former Piedmont High three-star football recruit Patrick Selna who signed with UCLA. Patch, we think you made the right call.

articles.text: Sunday’s rain was the heaviest in months for the Bay Area, which meant the Piedmont Post was out for another day of hiking. Walking to waterfalls is a joy during the winter season, and progressive rain should help the Bay Area recover from an extended drought. Last weekend we returned to Mt. Tamalpais in Marin County for a hike on the Cascade Falls and Carson Falls trails. Carson Falls is among the more popular destinations on Mt. Tam. The wet weather often deters others, creating some solitude for the lone, weather-resistant hiker. The weather allowed for opportune parking along Cascade Drive in Fairfax, which turns into the trailhead for Cascade Fire Road. The first landmark us about 0.7 mile away, Cascade Falls. The falls at this moment are more of a trickle due to the absence of rain for many months. Cascade Creek, however, is more of a treat with its bubbling brooks of running water from the falls. Walking back to the Cascade Fire Road is where our trek begins. 3.7 miles away is our second destination, the more popular and much more active Carson Falls. While the walk to Cascade Falls is level and easy, the hike to Carson Falls provides over 1,400 feet in elevation gain providing the chance for a good lower body workout. When totaling mile back to the car, you’re looking at around 2,100 feet in elevation gain in slightly less than nine miles. The trail goes along Cascade Creek on the way to Cascade Falls. A rocky road on the Cascade Falls Trail.

Tam’s Cascade & Carson Falls By Jonathan Comeaux Sunday’s rain was the heaviest in months for the Bay Area, which meant the Piedmont Post was out for another day of hiking. Walking to waterfalls is a joy during the winter season, and progressive rain should help the Bay Area recover from an extended drought. Last weekend we returned to Mt. Tamalpais in Marin County for a hike on the Cascade Falls and Carson Falls trails. Carson Falls is among the more popular destinations on Mt. Tam. The wet weather often deters others, creating some solitude for the lone, weather-resistant hiker. The weather allowed for opportune parking along Cascade Drive in Fairfax, which turns into the trailhead for Cascade Fire Road. The first landmark us about 0.7 mile away, Cascade Falls. The falls at this moment are more of a trickle due to the absence of rain for many months. Cascade Creek, however, is more of a treat with its bubbling brooks of running water from the falls. Walking back to the Cascade Fire Road is where our trek begins. 3.7 miles away is our second destination, the more popular and much more active Carson Falls. While the walk to Cascade Falls is level and easy, the hike to Carson Falls provides over 1,400 feet in elevation gain providing the chance for a good lower body workout. When totaling mile back to the car, you’re looking at around 2,100 feet in elevation gain in slightly less than nine miles. The trail goes along Cascade Creek on the way to Cascade Falls. A rocky road on the Cascade Falls Trail. The hike along the Cascade Fire Road doesn’t provide much coverage, so remember proper attire if out in the rain. The fire road is a hard red dirt road, packed down from mountain bikers that usually roam the area. Merging with Pine Mountain Road, the road will be covered with loose rocks that could cause tired hikers to trip if they aren’t paying attention. Those hiking in wet weather will be wise to watch where they put their feet over each stone, but doing so will enable them to the shimmering colors of the rocks beneath them on Pine Mountain Road. Glistening in the water are batches of greenstone that has an unmistakable golden glitter. You’ll also see the state rock of California, the green serpentine. Turning onto the Oak Hill Fire Road will lead you to the Carson Falls Trail, going back under some trees for a brief time until reaching the top of the falls. The roar of water when approaching will provide some excitement after the strenuous hike. The wet weather reduced the number of hikers. We saw only 19 people in the nine miles of hiking on a Sunday starting at 10:30 a.m. Nearly half of those were in the last couple of miles of when re-approaching the Cascade Falls Trailhead. Punch in “Cascade Canyon Open Space Preserve” to access this trailhead. There is also access to the trail off of the Fairfax-Bolinas Road for a quicker route to Carson Falls. A small amount of water creates Cascade Falls even now during a drought. The trail turns into a red dirt road along the Cascade Canyon Fire Road. The hike goes uphill with 2,100 feet in elevation gain throughout the day. Pine Mountain Road becomes a rocky gravel road. After stretches without tree cover, you’ll find some shade on the Carson Falls trail.

articles.text: I signed up for the Idioterod, I did. Now I wish I’d rode Idiot Airways instead. My huskies didn’t mush, but ran away. I wish I looked up the correct spelling. Iditarod is with and A, unlike any of my grades in cool weather self-preservation school. I suppose if I freeze I’ll be preserved well indeed. And to think, it’s just me. All the dogs ran home free, thankfully they are not stuck in this mound Of snow, sleet, ice, slush, powder and more snow. I must have been mentally sidetracked, and so went my sled. I headed off course, headed north, north, norse. But here come some funny looking deer and a warm coat of red held by little green men, so near. I may be losing my mind, but I think my saviors I did find. Go with the green men I shall; now we do fly. And I know not why but as I leave the snow With joy I yell out, “Ho! Ho! Ho!”

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet is presenting an archival performance of A Midsummer Night’s Dream available online from January 21 through February 10. Choreographer George Balanchine’s classic ballet, A Midsummer Night’s Dream, is part of San Francisco Ballet’s 2021 digital season, and will be performed in Program 1. The ballet, one of the company’s most well-known, is a Shakespearean favorite making its triumphant return to San Francisco after its run in 2020 was cut short due to COVID. This 1962 work by Balanchine, to music by Felix Mendelssohn, was his first original full-length ballet and quickly was hailed as a masterpiece. Balanchine loved the original play – he could recite large parts of it in Russian – so the ballet sticks close to its inspiration, telling the story of four lost lovers in the woods, as well as of a royal fairy court made up of Queen Titania, King Oberon, and the mischievous Puck. To obtain tickets to this digital event, visit https://www.sfballet. org/tickets/2021-season/. articles.text: Join Musaics of the Bay for a cross-continental celebration of the New Year, filmed in Salzburg, Austria, one of the capitals of the world for classical music. The New Year’s celebration is part of Musaics of the Bay’s “Stay-at-Home Symposium,” a series of broadcasts featuring music premieres based on the creativity of community members. It is a collaboration among composers, performers, artists of all types, and community members near and far. To date, the series has featured artists from Wales, Greece, Holland, and now, Austria. Musaics is partnering with Salzburg artists, including pianist Andrei Gologan, composer and violinist Luke Hsu, and cellist Simon Tetzlaff. The program features works by Beethoven, Kodaly, Schumann, and Luke Hsu, whose Pianist Andrei Gologan new composition was inspired by “Homage to Edmundo” by painter Darril Tighe. The concert will be recorded in High Definition and will livestream on Saturday, January 2, at 11 a.m. PST. articles.text: World-renowned mezzo-soprano Susan Graham leads the cast of Opera San Jose’s first fully staged digital production. Three Decembers, based on playwright Terrence McNally’s unpublished play Some Christmas Letters, and written by Bay Area composer Jake Heggie, stars world-renowned mezzo soprano Susan Graham. It will be conducted by Christopher James Ray, and directed by Tara Branham. The opera was first presented under the working title “Last Acts” at its world premiere by the Houston Grand Opera. A 10-instrument chamber orchestra included two pianos played by Heggie and Patrick Summers, who also conducted the performance in Houston. The 90-minute chamber opera explores a family’s struggle to understand one another. The three parts of the opera are set in the month of December in the years 1986, 1996, and 2006. Three Decembers follows the story of a famous actress, Madeline Mitchell, in a role sung by Graham. Two adult children, Beatrice and Charlie, are portrayed by Opera San Jose Resident Artists Maya Kherani and Efrain Solis. Graham will be making her company debut at Opera San Jose as Madeline, reuniting with composer Heggie, who created the role of Sister Helen in Dead Man Walking specifically for her. Three Decembers began streaming on December 3 and will continue through the end of the month. It will feature a virtual post-show conversation with Graham, Heggie, and the full artistic team. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré The New York Fashion industry. What comes to mind? Haute couture? Runways with tall, thin models draped in clothes that will never appear on any street, in any city, other than New York? Are creators of fashion involved in a headlong pursuit of the frivolous, far removed from life as most people live it? Or is fashion design as much an engine of creativity as any art form? After all, aren’t the ripples of its designs felt, however obliquely, in all of the clothes we choose to wear? A blouse by any other name – Prada, Gucci, Karan, Ford, Klein – is still a blouse. Right? Well, yes and no. But what is the connection between the industry and those sweatshops where people labor over sewing machines, stitching the garments that appear at shows and on the cover of major magazines? The documentary The September Issue, which is about fashion, does not address any of those questions. It does, however, offer an interesting glimpse behind the scenes of Vogue, the most influential fashion magazine being produced today. And the film draws an interesting portrait of its editor-in-chief, Anna Wintour, high priestess of fashion, examining how she marshals her large staff of designers, editors and photographers in a complex effort to produce the September issue, a signature fashion tome the size of a city phone book, weighing some four pounds. The September Issue is revelatory, but not as might be anticipated. It actually morphs into a character study of Wintour’s creative director, Grace Coddington, who has been with Wintour for more than 20 years. While Wintour is meticulously coiffed and dressed, Coddington, who walks the corridors of high fashion, is all but frumpy, her hair flaming-red, wild, her face deeply lined, her dresses shapeless, shod in practical sandals. She’s the antithesis of Vogue. She is also a strong woman with strong points of view and is fearless in her willingness to confront Wintour. Yet these two women have an alliance that is unwavering, sharing a mission to produce a stunningly beautiful magazine, Anna Wintour, Bee Shaffer and Karl Lagerfeld in The September Issue. Anna Wintour in The September Issue. Vera Wang and André Leon Talley in The September Issue. as rich in color and design as the styles that appear in its pages. The film is also a study of work. How people of far ranging abilities and egos and quirks manage to collaborate as the day of the magazine’s release draws ever nearer. The world of work is high fashion, Byzantine, intricate, the magazine unparalleled; yet the dynamics are essentially the same in any work place where people must co-exist in pursuit of a goal. articles.text: The city of Genova. on Italy’s northwestern coast, is a fabulously wealthy city. It was the birthplace of the explorer Christopher Columbus and violinist Niccolò Paganini. As you walk along Corso Garibaldi you can see some of those beautiful palaces. One of them is now Genoa’s City Hall. Its most famous piece of art is the Guarnerius violin of Paganini. Just down the street is an equally beautiful palace, but no one goes there. In its archives are the strings of Paganini‘s magic violin. The strings have a story to tell, one blessed by music and magic. Long ago in ancient Egypt, a music loving pharaoh had a harp made for him, but it was not just any old harp. This one was truly special – it was made of pure silver. The pharaoh made sure this particular harp was special and had it blessed by all of his priests. Some time later the great Jewish king, King David, obtained this special harp. And with it he sang his immortal songs. When the Romans put down the Jewish rebellion, they stole the harp and brought it to Rome. Emperor Nero became enamored with the harp. It was really this silver harp that he played and not that silly story of him fiddling on a violin while Rome burned. The harp remained in Italy and eventually became the instrument of the great operatic castrato FariPortait of young Niccolò Paganini nelli. Since Farinelli did not have any children, he gave the harp to a woman who was a brilliant noblewoman and socialite. She liked money more than she liked music and had the harp melted down and made into silver coins. After she died, her possessions were sold at auction. The most prominent Italian maker of violin strings went to the auction where he purchased a bag of silver coins. He used the silver to make some special violin strings for the great Paganini, and with these strings Paganini enchanted the world. After his death in 1840, Paganini requested that his violin be sent to Genoa. It is proudly displayed in the City Hall. It was the birthplace of the explorer Christopher Columbus and violinist Niccolò Paganini. As you walk along Corso Garibaldi you can see some of those beautiful palaces. One of them is now Genoa’s City Hall. Its most famous piece of art is the Guarnerius violin of Paganini. Just down the street is an equally beautiful palace, but no one goes there. In its archives are the strings of Paganini‘s magic violin. The strings have a story to tell, one blessed by music and magic. Long ago in ancient Egypt, a music loving pharaoh had a harp made for him, but it was not just any old harp. This one was truly special – it was made of pure silver. The pharaoh made sure this particular harp was special and had it blessed by all of his priests. Some time later the great Jewish king, King David, obtained this special harp. And with it he sang his immortal songs. When the Romans put down the Jewish rebellion, they stole the harp and brought it to Rome. Emperor Nero became enamored with the harp. It was really this silver harp that he played and not that silly story of him fiddling on a violin while Rome burned. The harp remained in Italy and eventually became the instrument of the great operatic castrato FariPortait of young Niccolò Paganini nelli. Since Farinelli did not have any children, he gave the harp to a woman who was a brilliant noblewoman and socialite. She liked money more than she liked music and had the harp melted down and made into silver coins. After she died, her possessions were sold at auction. The most prominent Italian maker of violin strings went to the auction where he purchased a bag of silver coins. He used the silver to make some special violin strings for the great Paganini, and with these strings Paganini enchanted the world. After his death in 1840, Paganini requested that his violin be sent to Genoa. It is proudly displayed in the City Hall. The strings from that violin are in another palace down the street but are hidden from public view – silent once again. And now you know the entire story. Runways with tall, thin models draped in clothes that will never appear on any street, in any city, other than New York? Are creators of fashion involved in a headlong pursuit of the frivolous, far removed from life as most people live it? Or is fashion design as much an engine of creativity as any art form? After all, aren’t the ripples of its designs felt, however obliquely, in all of the clothes we choose to wear? A blouse by any other name – Prada, Gucci, Karan, Ford, Klein – is still a blouse. Right? Well, yes and no. But what is the connection between the industry and those sweatshops where people labor over sewing machines, stitching the garments that appear at shows and on the cover of major magazines? The documentary The September Issue, which is about fashion, does not address any of those questions. It does, however, offer an interesting glimpse behind the scenes of Vogue, the most influential fashion magazine being produced today. And the film draws an interesting portrait of its editor-in-chief, Anna Wintour, high priestess of fashion, examining how she marshals her large staff of designers, editors and photographers in a complex effort to produce the September issue, a signature fashion tome the size of a city phone book, weighing some four pounds. The September Issue is revelatory, but not as might be anticipated. It actually morphs into a character study of Wintour’s creative director, Grace Coddington, who has been with Wintour for more than 20 years. While Wintour is meticulously coiffed and dressed, Coddington, who walks the corridors of high fashion, is all but frumpy, her hair flaming-red, wild, her face deeply lined, her dresses shapeless, shod in practical sandals. She’s the antithesis of Vogue. She is also a strong woman with strong points of view and is fearless in her willingness to confront Wintour. Yet these two women have an alliance that is unwavering, sharing a mission to produce a stunningly beautiful magazine, Anna Wintour, Bee Shaffer and Karl Lagerfeld in The September Issue. Anna Wintour in The September Issue. Vera Wang and André Leon Talley in The September Issue. as rich in color and design as the styles that appear in its pages. The film is also a study of work. How people of far ranging abilities and egos and quirks manage to collaborate as the day of the magazine’s release draws ever nearer. The world of work is high fashion, Byzantine, intricate, the magazine unparalleled; yet the dynamics are essentially the same in any work place where people must co-exist in pursuit of a goal. articles.text: Film directors Nicole Newnham and Jim LeBrecht. No one at Camp Jened could’ve imagined that those summers in the woods together would be the beginnings of a revolution. Just down the road from Woodstock, Camp Jened was a camp for disabled teens. Directors Nicole Newnham and Jim LeBrecht deliver a rousing film about a group of campers turned activists who shaped the future of the disability rights movement and changed accessibility legislation for everyone. Filled with the spirit, music, and humor of the era, Newnham and LeBrecht speak firsthand to the seeds of empowerment that were planted at Camp Jened. Footage from 1971 captures how the campers were finally seen beyond their disabilities. Milestones in the disability-rights movement intersect with LeBrecht’s personal story and the stories of several Camp Jened alums, including then-counselor Judy Heumann. She went on to play an indispensable role in historic protests leading to the Americans with Disabilities Act. Crip Camp shines a bright light on an overlooked civil-rights battle. Crip Camp acquires breadth and seriousness that neither its early scenes nor its playfully confrontational title suggest. As we follow campers into direct actions, occupations and unsparing encounters with government officials, the film’s approach remains anecdotal and emotional. Footage of a twenty-something Judy Heumann reproaching Eugene Eidenberg from the U.S. Department of Health is a master class in focused, righteous rage. Heumann went on to advise Presidents Clinton and Obama. Crip Camp opened the Sundance Film Festival and took home the Audience Award as Best Documentary. The film was produced by Barack and Michelle Obama under their production company Higher Ground. articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Pom Poko. Movie review by Chris Honoré Pom Poko is a strange, convoluted film, perhaps best suited for teens and adults. And even then its audience may indeed be those who have find pleasure in taking a deep dive into the extraordinary work that has, for decades, been the signature of Studio Ghibli. The hand-drawn animation of Pom Poko is remarkable, wrapped in wonderfully imagined moments. However, the weakness of Pom Poko resides not with its art, but in the storytelling. First, you should know that the words Pom Poko refer to what are called, in Japanese mythology, tanuki, or “raccoon dogs”. They look like a cross between a raccoon and a wolverine, thought to be as amiable as a hedgehog, with huge pouches. These raccoons are said to be mischievous and capable of using the “illusion science” of shape-shifting wherein they can transform themselves into anthropomorphic animals. The story begins in 1960 when the habitat of the tanuki is threatened by a giant subdivision, called Tama Hills, on the outskirts of Tokyo, causing distress for not only the forest wildlife, but most especially the tanuki. The story resumes some 30 years later when the tanuki matriarch, Oroku (Tess MacNeille), plus the war-like chief, Gonta (Clancy Brown), and the resourceful Shoukichi (Jonathan Taylor Thomas) urge the A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Pom Poko. tribe to resist the expanding encroachment. And so begins the confrontation between the tanuki and the developers, realistic and cartoonish, occasionally spiced up with trickery, as when some tanuki go undercover, shape-shifting to appear human while roaming the urban streets. The threads that stich the narrative together, both melodramatic and cartoonish, are numerous, often lack focus, and are, on occasion, leavened by slapstick and light-hearted fantasy. At one point, a pageant of mystical creatures are on parade, as well as a huge tsunami, both intended to scare the construction crews and the townies. This tanuki strategy also includes construction-site sabotage that does frighten and even kills some of the workers. Much of Pom Poko is surreal, at times manic, relying on the sustained attempt by the tanuki to terrorize the humans. It’s a spectacle, a somewhat grim tale, leading to a dour denouement which sums up what proves to be a not family friendly fable framed by bizarre moments that can only be described as culturally curious. Pom Poko (1994), Animé from Studio Ghibli. Directed by Isao Takahata. With the voices of Jonathan Taylor Thomas, Clancy Brown, Tess MacNeille and Andre Stojka. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Spirit of the American City (https://catherineburns.com/ spirit) is an online exhibit by Catherine Burns Fine Art that invites viewers to explore early 20th century prints through the perspective of period photography. See what the artists saw. Understand their inspiration. View them as a social time capsule while admiring the mastery of these revered printmakers. What makes this show special? This is the first time that original prints have been paired with related videos and historic photographs. From a private East Coast collection, these outstanding prints are by a wide range of well-known WPA period printmakers, including Edward Hopper, George Bellows, Charles Sheeler, Benton Spruance and Childe Hassam. Every print has been researched in detail and is accompanied by a mix of vintage photos, historic videos and news articles that give hints to what led the artists to capture that specific image in time. Not just for collectors This is a show for all to enjoy and is a breath of fresh air. Launched on November 20 to a select group, the show has received rave reviews from leading print experts: “The feedback from the show has been extraordinary,” said Burns, a 35-year veteran in the art world. “The inspiration for the show was to find a way to make hundred-yearold prints a momentary escape from the doom and gloom of the pandemic. A love letter to the artists and the cities that inspired them.” The show is online and free to the public at https://catherineburns.com/spirit. It is best enjoyed on a large screen. All of the featured prints are for sale. Catherine Burns has been a dealer in fine prints and drawings for more than 30 years and specializes in both American and European prints from the 19th and early 20th centuries. She launched her business after serving as the Curator of the art museums at University of Massachusetts, Amherst and Washington University in St. Louis. A founding member of the International Fine Print Dealers Association, Burns exhibits at national and international art fairs. To view her gallery and for more information, contact her at info@catherineburns.com, or call 510-654-7910.

articles.text: Once a city has imaginative architects and designers working with receptive owners and skilled craftsmen, the result is often the creation of what I am referring to as design “punctuation points”. Walking around Piedmont it is easy to come across examples of punctuation that add so much interest and personality to all parts of our city. At the core of their work, all of the design professions balance the combination of functional requirements with an aesthetic concept. You may be familiar with the famous maxim, “Form follows function.” attributed to the influential Chicago architect Louis Sullivan in 1896. Because there are of course many different attitudes towards aesthetics and decoration (Form), this famous maxim has been interpreted, reinterpreted and argued over for generations. In the aesthetic half of the equation there are time-tested rules of order that make for appealing designs. But, as we have discussed in previous columns, there are also exceptions to every design norm, and often these exceptions are, well, exceptional! They can provide surprisingly wonderful results that, even though different and even sometimes contradictory, can punctuate the main design and contribute greatly to the spirit and visual character of our built environment. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had its Zoom book discussion on December 7, with 14 readers on the call to discuss Jane Austen’s classic novel, Pride and Prejudice. Some members of the group also read Longbourn by Jo Baker, which describes events in Pride and Prejudice from the perspectives of the house servants. Participating in the discussion were Mike Bandrowski, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Alicia Rivera, Jeri Lockhart, Margie Blodgett, Dick Carter, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. The group was also pleased to welcome first time participant Bill Blackwell. Pride and Prejudice, a romantic novel, was first published in 1813. Austen set the story at the turn of the 19th century, and it follows the main character, Elizabeth Bennet, as she deals with issues of manners, upbringing, morality, education, and marriage in the society of the landed gentry of Britain. Elizabeth’s father, Mr. Bennet, has five daughters, but his Longbourn estate property can only be passed to a male heir. His wife also lacks an inheritance, so his family will be destitute upon his death. Therefore, at least one of the girls must marry well to support the others. The novel revolves around the importance of marrying for love, rather than money or social prestige, despite the pressure to find a wealthy husband. Pride and Prejudice has consistently appeared near the top of lists of “most-loved books.” It is one of the most popular novels in English literature with over 20 million copies sold. Austen and the book are certainly loved by many of the members of the reading group. Alicia Rivera suggested that a Jane Austen novel be read by the group every December as a holiday tradition. Laura Goldman read it while doing some historical research. The novel was set in a time of the Napoleonic Wars when a great many potentially eligible English bachelors were killed. Finding an appropriate husband was made all the more difficult for the Bennets. It accounted for the presence of the nearby militia that are an important feature of the novel. During these times a person and family’s reputation and standing were very important in the quest for a husband. This accounted for the Bennet family’s trauma when one of the daughters ran off with an unprincipled army soldier. While Pride and Prejudice was appreciated by all members of th reading group, some readers found it a bit of a soap opera with challenging language that was at times hard to follow. Others found this to be part of the book’s charm. There seemed to be a slight difference in the enjoyment of the book between the women and men, with the women enjoying it more. Those who also read Jo Baker’s Longbourn found it to be an interesting complement with striking differences in language, some sordid behind-the-scenes revelations, and greater sympathy for the flighty Mrs. Bennet and her need for a son, or son-in-law. Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austen. With their book discussion complete, the group discussed future books to read. They had previously decided to continue their social justice exploration in January with the selection of How to be an Anti-Racist by Ibram X. Kendi. For February and March, they had also selected the novels, Olive Again by Elizabeth Strout and Drive Your Plow over the Bones of the Dead by Polish author Olga Tokarczuk. However, they added Olive Kitteridge to the February reading. This is the first “Olive” novel by Elizabeth Strout. Assuming social distancing is still in place, the group will meet next in a Zoom call on Monday, January 4, at 1:30 p.m. New members are always welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required by contacting John Wilk at the Piedmont Recreation Department at jwilk@ piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: As the year draws to a close, it’s fair to say that we’ve all learned something about the social, political, physical and environmental forces that have affected everyone. In some ways our lives will be changed, perhaps permanently. But as an investor, what lessons can you learn from 2020? Here are some to consider: • Markets look ahead Here’s something many investors discovered in 2020: Investment prices don’t always move in the same direction as the overall economy. This might not have seemed apparent right after the COVID-19 pandemic struck in mid-February, as the overall economy and the stock market took big hits. But just about five weeks later, the markets began a rally that lasted several months. During this time, the economy also recovered somewhat, but still remains on weak footing. What can explain this discrepancy between the markets and economic activity? Essentially, economic numbers, such as the unemployment rate and gross domestic product (GDP), reflect what’s happening today, but the markets are always looking toward tomorrow, which means they are anticipating a stronger economic recovery and the results that come with it, such as greater corporate earnings in 2021. No one can say for sure what the future holds, but you can usually know the market’s opinion by its performance. • Opportunities will always exist for investors Although the coronavirus seems unprecedented, the equity markets have rebounded from many crises before it. From war to global financial meltdowns, the market has seen it all. But even at the height of these events, when the markets might be most affected, individual segments or industries can do well. For example, in the current environment, when many people have been forced to work and shop from home, and get their entertainment online, it’s probably not surprising that some parts of the technology sector have seen their economic activity grow, along with their stock prices. Here’s the key point: Investment opportunities always exist, especially in times of market stress – and smart investors will find them and incorporate them into their portfolios in a way that’s appropriate for their goals and risk tolerance. • Patience and discipline can pay dividends As mentioned above, the stock market dropped sharply in the weeks immediately following the pandemic, but then gained steadily for months afterward. Investors who tried to “cut losses” and exited the market likely did so at the wrong time and missed out on the beginning of the upturn. Unfortunately, this is not uncommon; investors who overreact to market declines often find themselves on the investment sidelines just when a new rally begins. Rather than being reactive in this way, you may be better off sticking with a longterm investment strategy, and buying and selling investments only when it makes sense for your situation, such as when you need to diversify your portfolio. For many reasons, it’s unlikely that we’ll see anything exactly like 2020 again. But some of the investment lessons we learned are applicable in every year – so keep them in mind for 2021 and beyond. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. Because of the unique situation of two councilmembers being nominated for the position, City Attorney Michelle Kenyon, who was present, clarified that the council must first consider the nomination of Cavenaugh. If that motion did not pass, then the council would move to the second nomination of Rood, and then a motion and vote would be taken for that. A majority vote was needed to appoint a vice mayor. “This should not be a popularity contest. What I like about our tradition is that it is not a popularity contest among councilmembers, it’s the most votes,” Andersen reiterated. She added that her nomination for King as mayor followed that tradition. In response, McCarthy said that she would “absolutely welcome a conversation about the process,” but that she did not see a current one that was workable. Cavenaugh said that the meeting was supposed to be a “fairly straightforward session based on a long-established tradition,” and that the city did in fact have a clear process. “In the past, our vice mayor has always been the person next in line to be mayor, who is also the person with the greatest seniority at that time. When [there are] two people who have that, we look at the vote count,” she said. This would naturally leave a councilmember “out,” who would not have a chance to serve as mayor or vice mayor. “When we talk about vote count, what that really reflects is the will of the voters,” Cavenaugh added. McCarthy, in response to the tradition of top vote-getting, said that a “vote for council is not a vote for mayor.” She said that she did not want to move forward with the nomination of Cavenaugh with the information presented by her colleagues. The motion to nominate Cavenaugh failed, 2-2. McCarthy and King dissented. Discussion on the nomination of Rood, who was not present for the agenda item due to a work conflict, then transpired. Had Rood been there and voted for himself to take the position, the nomination would have passed 3-2 without conflict. Andersen acknowledged Rood’s qualifications but stayed firm in her stance on sticking to tradition. Cavenaugh suggested exploring one-year mayoral and vice mayoral terms in the future, but also stayed firm in her decision. King reiterated that she felt it was her responsibility to hear Rood’s stance, because he had explicitly expressed an interest in the position. “I want to let him have the chance to make his case, and from my perspective, [the council] owes him that,” she said. The motion to nominate Rood also failed, 2-2, with Andersen and Cavenaugh dissenting. Andersen then nominated a shared vice mayorship, “whereby Rood is vice mayor for one year, and we have Cavenaugh as vice mayor for the second year.” “This might be an elegant solution to the position we find ourselves in this evening,” she offered. McCarthy agreed, saying it was a good solution. King seconded Andersen’s motion, and the motion passed 3-1, with Cavenaugh opposing. Little discussion followed Andersen’s motion. The vote means that immediately following Rood’s one-year tenure as vice mayor, which starts this month, Cavenaugh would take over the position. The only written indication of a process in city code states that, “following each general municipal election, the City Council shall elect from among its member officers of the City who shall have the titles of Mayor and ViceMayor, each of whom shall serve at the pleasure of the Council.” During the December 7 meeting, councilmember Andersen suggested making the process more concrete. If the newly configured city council decides to do so, it would be the first written guidelines in the city for selecting a vice mayor.
